fieldValues.title: The level test: a spec rule must be declarable and checkable, or it is an authoring rule
fieldValues.decision_rationale:
srs#812's meaning-placement sweep found the spec asserting rules that no repository can declare and no implementation can check. The owner's example is the sharpest: `contains` has exactly one parent is load-bearing (I-148, I-66, RFC-042 [R2]) and this repository obeys it perfectly across 542 edges, yet nothing in SRS made it so. Relation validation is exactly E1-E4 in crates/srs-core/src/validation/relation.rs; `repo validate` has no cardinality, tree-shape or cycle check for any relation type; `RelationTypeDefinition` exposes only `irreflexive` and `requireSameType`. The rule is held up entirely by scripts/check-spec-coherence.mjs check (2), a bespoke Node script binding this repository and no other. So a rule about how we write the spec sits in the spec as though it constrained every SRS user, and it repeats about nineteen times.

The principle that resolves this was already ruled, for one clause of one record, by rfc-decision-1e7c0c8e. It never generalised, and the compass has no section for the distinction, so each unit re-derives it from scratch - the drift shape the charter names as "a rule stated once, remaining sites silent". Design-note 044 R10 already supplies the removal half of the test ("a principle stated in prose but enforced nowhere is a defect, to be enforced or removed") but not the hold half, and the removal half alone would cut rules whose only defect is that the machinery is unbuilt. The owner's ruling states the test and adds the third disposition that keeps it from being a demolition order.
fieldValues.decision_statement:
A normative statement belongs in the SRS specification only if some repository can DECLARE it through SRS machinery and some implementation can CHECK it. If it can only be obeyed, it is an authoring or governance rule and lives at that level - this repository's spec-language guide, or the charter. Declarable and checkable are one conjunction: a constraint nobody can state in a repository's own data is not made normative by an implementation enforcing it, and a constraint that is declarable but that no implementation reads is an affordance without a contract (layer rule 6), not a rule.

This generalises rfc-decision-1e7c0c8e from the one clause it was written for into a standing placement test. That record ruled, of rfc-decision-5f8204bc's instance clause alone, verbatim: "The standard and its tooling provide mechanisms for retiring instances ... and enforce nothing beyond honesty about what each mechanism does. ... A generic tool defines what is possible, not what every corpus must do with it." The principle was never clause-specific; only its application was. It is now a test asked of every normative statement, at Charter Check time and at review, alongside the cell check and the layer test.

A rule that fails the test has three dispositions, not two. It may be RELOCATED to the level that owns it, where it keeps its force over this repository and loses its false claim over every other. It may be RETIRED outright, where a declarable construct already does its work. Or it may be HELD. A rule is held when it is a mechanism we intend to build: it stays in the spec unenforced, and the change that holds it names the machinery that would carry it and the issue that owes it, joining the make-it-real queue. A held rule is a debt with a named payer, never an exemption; if the machinery is declined, the rule falls back to relocation or retirement. Without the hold disposition the test reads as a demolition order, and that is not what is ruled here.

This is not the sanctioned two-tier boundary that rfc-decision-43249f53 rejected, and the objection is answered rather than set aside. That record refused two tiers of one mechanism - a bare status enum for light cases, a Lifecycle when transitions matter - on the ground that "the two-tier boundary would itself become a drift seam": authors would drift across the line case by case, and the same job would be done two ways inside SRS. Nothing here is two-tiered. There is one mechanism, SRS's declarable and checkable machinery, and separately one document-authoring convention that this repository writes by and that no SRS implementation reads. They do not compete for the same job, and they do not sit in the same repository's scope: SRS neither requires nor forbids the authoring convention of anyone else, and the convention claims no conformance force over anyone, including us. The seam 43249f53 feared runs inside a single mechanism; the line drawn here is the boundary between a mechanism and a house style, which is the boundary one-way-per-goal exists to keep clean rather than a breach of it. Where the two could genuinely blur is a held rule, which by construction sits in the spec while its machinery is unbuilt - which is why a hold must name its machinery and its issue, so the blur has an end date instead of a habit.
fieldValues.decision_scope: The placement of normative statements on the SRS specification's normative surface - the record Types that scripts/spec-language-registry.json declares normative (com.semanticops.spec/invariant and com.semanticops.spec/mechanism) and the conformance rules of accepted RFCs. This record's own level is repository governance (Governance); it binds the authoring of this specification and corpora that adopt this charter, not SRS implementations, and it creates no load-time invariant and no new check. It does not rule the disposition of any individual existing rule: the sweep that applies the test is srs#818, the authoring guide that receives what it relocates is srs#819, and the RFC that would discharge the held rules is srs#820. rfc-decision-1e7c0c8e's own application to rfc-decision-5f8204bc's instance clause, and every scoping clause 1e7c0c8e states about 5f8204bc, stand exactly as ratified; what this record changes is the reach of the principle, not any disposition 1e7c0c8e made under it.
fieldValues.alternatives_considered: (1) Leave rfc-decision-1e7c0c8e clause-scoped and apply its principle ad hoc, unit by unit. Rejected: that is the status quo, and it is what produced about nineteen restatements of one authoring rule as universal spec text; a principle with no section in the compass is re-derived (or not) by every reader, which is the drift shape the charter names. (2) State the test with two dispositions only - relocate or retire - which is what design-note 044 R10 says on its own. Rejected by the owner: it would cut rules whose only defect is that the machinery is unbuilt (RFC-042 [R2] single-parent, precedes acyclicity, the naming grammar of mechanism-b3c293f9), turning an honesty measure into a demolition order and foreclosing the very capabilities srs#820 exists to add. (3) Make the test a mechanical check rather than a review test. Rejected: "can some repository declare this" has no machine predicate today, and a guard that could be written would only re-express the reviewer's judgement as a keyword scan - the observability-pressure audit's own warning about citing a test without honouring it. (4) Treat this as a correction to rfc-decision-1e7c0c8e rather than a successor. Rejected under rfc-decision-4431046e's test: a reader acting on 1e7c0c8e as written applies it to rfc-decision-5f8204bc's instance clause and nothing else; a reader acting on this record applies it to every normative statement in the spec. The position's reach changed, so it ships as a successor record and 1e7c0c8e is never edited.
fieldValues.accepted_costs: The test is a review test, not a guard: like the cell check and the layer test it can be cited without being honoured, and "declarable and checkable" is judged by a reviewer. No check is added here, and the charter gains a rule whose observability is the hard-to-verify kind the 2026-08-23 observability-pressure audit warns bites first. The hold disposition is the pressure point, because held is the comfortable answer for any rule someone would rather not cut; it is legitimate only with the machinery and the issue named, and a hold whose issue closes without the machinery is a finding, not a settled exemption. Relocating rules off the normative surface also means a conformant implementation is no longer told to enforce them - accepted deliberately, since no implementation could enforce them in the first place and the core conformance profile that enumerated them was therefore unsatisfiable.

fieldValues.review_trigger: Review when SRS gains declared structural constraints (srs#820) - acyclicity, cardinality, endpoint-type restriction, uniqueness-within-scope - because every rule held on that machinery then becomes declarable and must move from held to enforced, or be retired. Review also when a held rule's named machinery issue closes without the machinery having been built: that converts a debt into the standing exemption this record refuses, and the held rule falls back to relocation or retirement rather than staying on the normative surface unexamined.
